name: Belt pulling (CCW rotation bonesmash)

lead: Belt pulling is a looksmaxxing routine in which a person grips a belt in the mouth and applies body-weight force upward and forward. Proponents say this rotates the maxilla counterclockwise, which in their account shortens the midface, supports the under-eye area and brings the lower jaw forward.

It is discussed alongside towel pulling, thumb pulling and mewing as a non-surgical alternative to jaw surgery. Orthodontists use supervised facemask devices on growing children for related goals, but no published trial has tested the belt method.

paras: Forum descriptions involve a belt hung from a fixed point near mouth height, biting it, tucking the chin and loading body weight. Proponents pair it with proper tongue posture and say results take months. These accounts are not endorsed here.

Forum users report cracking sounds in the jaw, nausea, and teeth moving forward rather than any visible bone change. Commenters on looksmax.org warn that teeth shift far more easily than bone. Orthodontic headgear itself has reported side effects, including tooth soreness and, rarely, eye injuries, and is fitted by professionals.

chain: Bite a belt and apply upward traction
Claimed to rotate the maxilla counterclockwise
Shorter midface, more forward lower face
angle.text: Proponents use it to try to reshape the upper jaw without surgery. Their stated aim is a shorter midface, more under-eye support and a more forward mandible.

lead: Belt pulling, also written about as counterclockwise (CCW) maxillary rotation, is a do-it-yourself routine from looksmaxxing forums. Participants bite on a belt and pull with body weight in an attempt to rotate the upper jaw upward at the back and forward at the front, which they describe as counterclockwise when viewed from the side [1].

Proponents say that a downward-rotated maxilla produces a long midface, weak under-eye support and a recessed-looking jaw, and that rotating it back would fill the midface and move the mandible forward. They describe belt pulling as a free alternative to bimaxillary surgery and as a stronger version of mewing, often combined with thumb pulling, towel pulling and attention to tongue posture [1][2].

No clinical studies have examined belt pulling. The closest professional analogue is the orthodontic facemask, which is prescribed and monitored by an orthodontist to encourage forward maxillary growth in children [3].

paras: A forum guide describes the exercise as using a belt hung high, for example from a pull-up bar, with its lowest part near mouth height. The user bites the belt, tucks the chin and braces, and uses body weight to apply force. The author says it should be paired with proper tongue posture to stabilise results and calls it more effective than other face-pulling techniques for counterclockwise rotation [1].

Another thread presents the theory behind it: that downward maxillary rotation lengthens the midface, removes under-eye support and swings the jaw backward, so rotating the maxilla up and forward would address them. The poster calls it an extreme version of mewing and asks whether it is safe [2].
Proponents say belt pulling can fill the midface, lower the face's apparent length and benefit malocclusion [1]. They sometimes present it as a free alternative to bimaxillary osteotomy [2].

Orthodontists use a facemask or reverse-pull headgear, which attaches elastics to braces and anchors to the forehead and chin, to encourage forward growth of the maxilla in Class III cases. It is used mainly in children and adolescents, typically between about 7 and 13 years of age, and is fitted and adjusted by an orthodontist [3]. Wikipedia notes that such devices effectively pull the teeth forward and lists side effects including tooth soreness, eye injuries with improper use, and reports of breathing and jaw joint problems [3].

One forum user who tried the method reported that only the back teeth moved forward and the lips widened briefly, with a cracking sound in the jaw and nausea [4]. Other commenters wrote that force anchored on the teeth moves teeth rather than skeletal bone, and that the method is dangerous without professional guidance [2]. Some replies dismiss the approach as risky [1].

lore.intro: Belt pulling appears in looksmax.org threads as a more intense relative of mewing, discussed for rotated maxilla and midface concerns [1][2].
